Contributions from intensity factors ​

Before this page

Crack opening displacement and compliance §3, for      and the density of a crack family, and §7, for the intensity factors , and the energy release rate.

The closed forms of cover the ellipse and the ribbon. Many other cracks have known intensity factors: a crack bonded on part of its surface, a crack grown from a pore, a curved crack. This page turns intensity factors into a compliance contribution and a resistivity contribution , by integrating the energy released while the crack grows (Rice, 1975; Kachanov and Sevostianov, 2012). It then computes the intensity factors of the annular crack, which the literature gives only in the opening mode.

1. The energy released by a growing crack ​

A volume of a linear elastic solid of compliance carries a uniform remote stress . A crack grows in it from a nucleus, along a path indexed by  : at stage its front is the curve , of outer normal in the plane tangent to the crack, and the front advances along by  . The overall compliance of is , with  .

At fixed , the complementary energy of is    , and its increase is the energy released at the front, the energy release rate integrated over the area the front sweeps:

Integrated from the nucleus to the current crack, with   :

The energy release rate is a quadratic form in the stress intensity factor vector (§7 of the COD page),

being the COD tensor of the ribbon tangent to the front, of normal and width direction , for any anisotropy of the matrix. is linear in the remote stress:   , with a third-order influence tensor, symmetric in its last two indices. Both sides of (1) are then quadratic forms in the symmetric , and the fourth-order tensors with major and minor symmetries that represent them coincide:

where    is the fourth-order tensor such that          . For identical, non-interacting cracks per unit volume, of density   built on a length (  for a crack bounded in its plane,   for a crack unbounded along one direction), the dilute correction     of the COD page gives the contribution

being the factor of crack_density_factor ( or ). Two consequences follow. The result does not depend on the growth path, since the left side of (1) does not; and it is less sensitive to the details of the shape than the intensity factors themselves, which it integrates.

2. Flat cracks: back to the COD tensor ​

On a flat crack of normal , the problem is that of the faces loaded by   in an unloaded solid, so the intensity factors depend on   only:    . Then

and (3) takes the form      of the COD page, with

( ,   for a crack normalized as a penny). This is rice_cod_tensor: the user gives the front point by point, the matrix enters only through .

A penny-shaped crack grown from its center checks (4). At radius the front has  ,  ,   and, in an isotropic matrix of Young modulus and Poisson ratio (Kassir and Sih, 1966),

with    and   . Along the circle      , and (4) gives     , the closed form of the COD page. The same with the sliding modes, by RiceCrack:

julia
using MeanFieldHomogenization, TensND, Printf
E, ν = 1.0, 0.25
C₀ = iso_stiffness_E_nu(E, ν)
grown = RiceCrack(1.0;
    K_I   = (ρ, ν) -> 2sqrt(ρ / π),
    K_II  = (ρ, ν) -> 4sqrt(ρ / π) / (2 - ν),
    K_III = (ρ, ν) -> 4(1 - ν) * sqrt(ρ / π) / (2 - ν))
B_rice = TensND.canonical_components(cod_tensor(grown, C₀))
B_ref = TensND.canonical_components(cod_tensor(PennyCrack(1.0), C₀))
@printf "B_nn: %.12f (Rice)  %.12f (closed form)\n" B_rice[3, 3] B_ref[3, 3]
@printf "B_tt: %.12f (Rice)  %.12f (closed form)\n" B_rice[1, 1] B_ref[1, 1]
B_nn: 1.591549430919 (Rice)  1.591549430919 (closed form)
B_tt: 1.818913635336 (Rice)  1.818913635336 (closed form)

3. Conduction ​

In steady conduction (conventions of Notation,   ), an insulating crack carries at its front the flux intensity factor and the temperature jump   . The energy release rate is    , with   the thermal COD scalar of a ribbon in an isotropic conductor    (Thermal cracks). The argument of §1 holds word for word, with the resistivity in place of and   :

A flat crack has the same factor in both problems ​

For a flat crack in an isotropic matrix, the flux intensity factor per unit normal flux equals the stress intensity factor per unit normal stress:    . The two problems are written on the plane of the crack, with the two-dimensional Fourier transform of .

Opening. The opening (jump of  ) is symmetric: each half-space receives the normal displacement with no shear traction on the plane. The normal displacement of the surface of a half-space under a point force , normal to it, is (Love, 1927), whose transform is ; the traction normal to the plane and the opening are therefore related by   .

Conduction. The jump is symmetric as well: each half-space receives . A point source on the surface of a half-space raises its temperature by , of transform ; the flux across the plane and the jump are related by   .

On the crack, the opening answers     and the jump answers , outside it both vanish. The same operator, scaled by or , therefore gives    at every point. At the front this reads   , and with    and   :

4. The annular crack ​

The annular crack is a penny of radius whose faces are bonded on the central disc of radius : it occupies   . Its opening factors were tabulated by Smetanin (1968), with an accuracy of 1 % at the outer front and 2 % at the inner one; Kachanov and Sevostianov (2012) integrate them by (1) for . The sliding modes, which give the rest of , are computed here by a Galerkin method on the equation of the crack.

The equation of the crack in weak form ​

Let be the jump of displacement across the crack and the traction it induces on the plane of the crack in an unloaded isotropic solid. The faces are free, so     on the crack. The opening obeys §3:    . The sliding (in the plane) is antisymmetric: each half-space receives with no normal traction. A tangential point force on a half-space moves its surface by       in the plane (Love, 1927), of transform      ( the identity of the plane). Inverted, and with  :

Contracted with a test jump that vanishes on the front, transformed back by Parseval's identity, with     ,      and the transform of , the equation of the crack becomes, for every such ,

    being the scalar curl in the plane, and likewise        . The kernel   is only weakly singular, which is what makes this form fit a numerical solution.

Reduction to the radius ​

A uniform normal traction gives an axisymmetric opening . A uniform tangential traction   gives     , of   and   with    and   . The integrals over the angles leave the kernel

and the complete elliptic integrals, and the two equations

the subscript marking the test functions. Along the arithmetic–geometric mean started at ,    , the numerator is with   : a sum of positive terms, accurate at  .

Discretization and intensity factors ​

With    ,   ,   , each unknown is sought as , the Chebyshev polynomials of the second kind: the square root at both fronts is built in. The Galerkin system is assembled on the of  , where the derivatives of the unknowns are the Chebyshev polynomials . Near the outer front, at distance , a jump reads    , which gives the displacement intensity factor and, through   ,

( at the outer front, at the inner one). The error decreases as   ; is chosen accordingly, from 24 to 160.

julia
crack = AnnularCrack(1.0, 0.5)
Σ = TensND.Tens([0 0 0.3; 0 0 0; 0.3 0 1.0], crack_basis(crack))
for front in (:outer, :inner)
    _, (KI, KII, KIII) = sif(crack, C₀, Σ; front)
    @printf "%-5s front  K_I = %.6f  K_II = %+.6f  K_III = %+.6f\n" front KI KII KIII
end
outer front  K_I = 0.838122  K_II = +0.269436  K_III = +0.000000
inner front  K_I = 1.007828  K_II = -0.296808  K_III = +0.000000

The contribution ​

follows from (4) as the inner front grows from   (a circle of zero width) to  , the matrices being those of the penny with the factors of the annulus. Grown instead from the outer front, or read from the mean jumps of the final crack (   ), it is the same tensor:

julia
B1 = TensND.canonical_components(cod_tensor(crack, C₀))                     # Rice, inner front
B2 = TensND.canonical_components(cod_tensor(crack, C₀; method = :opening))  # mean jumps
@printf "B_nn = %.10f / %.10f   B_tt = %.10f / %.10f\n" B1[3, 3] B2[3, 3] B1[1, 1] B2[1, 1]
B_nn = 0.5606487195 / 0.5606487195   B_tt = 0.6493060636 / 0.6493060636

In conduction,   by §3.

5. The circular arc crack ​

A crack along the arc of circle of radius and half-angle , unbounded along the axis of the circle, is not flat and has no COD tensor: (3) applies with the whole influence tensor . In the frame of CircularArcCrack the arc is    ,  .

At the tip   the in-plane factors are (Sih et al., 1962; Cotterell and Rice, 1980), as written in (Kachanov and Sevostianov, 2018; eq. (1.9.27))

the other tip following by the mirror   . The anti-plane factor is that of the conduction problem with   (Kachanov and Sevostianov, 2018; eq. (1.10.9)):    . Both tips advance by  , and (2) integrates in closed form (Kachanov and Sevostianov, 2018; eqs. (1.9.28) and (1.10.12)). Per unit length of the axis, with   and   :

and   ,    . The arc is normalized as a ribbon of half-width :   and  . At   it is the ribbon; at   the cut core carries neither in-plane nor anti-plane stress, and the in-plane and anti-plane components are those of a cylindrical hole.

julia
arc = CircularArcCrack(1.0, 2π / 3)
H_closed = TensND.canonical_components(inverse_property_contribution(arc, C₀))
H_rice = TensND.canonical_components(inverse_property_contribution(arc, C₀; method = :rice))
@printf "H_nnnn = %.10f (closed form)  %.10f (Rice, numerical)\n" H_closed[3, 3, 3, 3] H_rice[3, 3, 3, 3]
H_nnnn = 0.5867878956 (closed form)  0.5867878956 (Rice, numerical)

6. The Saturn ring ​

A spherical pore of radius with an annular crack of length in its equatorial plane opens under a normal stress with   ,  , the factor fitted by Fett (1994) (Kachanov and Sevostianov, 2018; eqs. (4.4.16) and (4.4.17)). The ring is grown from the surface of the pore, its front at radius from to  , and by (4), in an isotropic matrix,

to which the pore adds its own contribution. Only the opening mode of this configuration is published, so only follows: saturn_ring_compliance.

julia
S = saturn_ring_compliance(1.0, 1.5, C₀)
@printf "pore %.6f  ring %.6f  total %.6f  penny of radius a + c: %.6f\n" S.pore S.ring S.total 16 * 2.5^3 * (1 - ν^2) / (3E)
pore 8.400346  ring 67.260616  total 75.660961  penny of radius a + c: 78.125000
